Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Rangi Taufa is a 63-year-old Tongan-American man who has been flying commercial aircraft for nearly three decades. He presents to the clinic with a PCL-5 score of 75, referred by his aviation medical examiner following a routine psychological screening that he had, for years, found ways to pass without full disclosure. He is married, softly spoken, and chooses his words with the careful precision one might expect from a man trained to communicate clearly under pressure. What he has not been able to communicate clearly, until now, is what has been happening inside him since a combat deployment in the early 1990s, when he served as a crew member aboard a military transport helicopter operating in a conflict zone in the Pacific theatre.

The event itself occurred in the early hours of the morning, before dawn had broken but after the deepest part of the night had passed — that particular grey, suspended hour when the sky is neither dark nor light. Rangi's helicopter had come under fire during what was meant to be a routine extraction. In the chaos that followed, he found himself pressing his hands against the torn flight suit of a fellow crew member, trying to hold pressure against a wound. He remembers the texture of that fabric — a rough, shredded weave soaked through — with a precision that has never dimmed. The man died before they reached the ground. Rangi was twenty-four years old.

In the months after his discharge, he completed his civilian pilot training and built what appeared from the outside to be an admirable life. He married, raised children, and accumulated tens of thousands of flight hours without incident. But certain things accumulated too. He noticed that his body responded to the sound of other aircraft — particularly helicopters — in ways he could not explain and did not discuss. Working out of a major hub airport, he encounters helicopter traffic regularly, and there are moments on the flight deck when a rotor sound cutting through the radio frequency or drifting up from the tarmac below will snap him somewhere else entirely, without transition, without warning. He has learned to grip the yoke and breathe and wait for it to pass, but he has never learned why it keeps happening. What frightened him most was not the memory itself but its arrival — sudden, total, and ungoverned.

At home, the hours around pre-dawn have always unsettled him in ways he attributed to shift work and irregular sleep. He does not name it as vigilance, but his wife has long known not to move quickly in the dark near him. Sudden movements from other people — a colleague reaching across him in the cockpit, a passenger rising unexpectedly from a seat during boarding — produce in him an immediate, full-body alertness that he has come to regard as simply part of who he is now. Whenever he enters a building, his eyes move to the exits before they move to anything else. He does this in hotel lobbies, in crew briefing rooms, in his own children's homes. He has come to believe that the world is genuinely dangerous in a way that others around him seem unable to perceive, and that this perception is not a symptom but a form of hard-won knowledge.

What troubles him most deeply is something harder to articulate. When he tries to think about the morning of the extraction, the memory feels as though it belongs to a different person entirely — a young man he can observe but not fully inhabit. And yet when the memory comes without his choosing, it brings the full terror of that moment as though no time has passed at all. He has come to believe that there is something fundamentally wrong with him, and that the man his wife married — the one who was, by his own account, genuinely happy — no longer exists.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was his upcoming mandatory retirement at sixty-five. For decades, the structure and identity of flying had contained something he could not name. Facing its loss, he found he could no longer afford not to know what he was carrying.
